groups.label: Headless, CI and the Agent SDK

concepts.s: Claude Code is one agent engine reachable from the terminal CLI, IDE extensions, a desktop app, the web and mobile, Slack and CI, and they all share the same CLAUDE.md, settings and MCP configuration.

x.b:
The Claude Code overview page describes it as an agentic coding tool that reads your codebase, edits files, runs commands and integrates with your tools. Each surface connects to the same engine, so your CLAUDE.md files, settings and MCP servers work across all of them.

  • Terminal CLI: the full-featured surface. The docs recommend the native installer (a curl of Anthropic's install.sh piped to bash on macOS, Linux and WSL, or a PowerShell script on Windows). Native installs auto-update in the background.
  • Homebrew: brew install --cask claude-code tracks a stable channel that the docs say is usually about a week behind and skips releases with major regressions; claude-code@latest tracks the newest. Homebrew and WinGet installs do not auto-update.
  • IDE: the VS Code extension (also installs in Cursor) gives inline diffs, @-mentions and plan review. The JetBrains plugin needs the CLI installed separately.
  • Desktop app: macOS and Windows, with Linux in beta. It bundles Claude Code and adds visual diff review, parallel sessions and scheduled tasks. It requires a paid subscription.
  • Web and mobile: claude.ai/code runs sessions in the cloud on a fresh clone, available in desktop browsers and the Claude iOS and Android apps.

The overview and Remote Control pages list these hand-offs:

  • Remote Control (claude remote-control, or /remote-control in Desktop and VS Code) lets a phone or browser drive a session that keeps executing on your machine. It needs a Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise login; API keys are not supported, and on Team and Enterprise an Owner must enable it.
  • Cloud to terminal: start a long task on the web or mobile and pull it local with claude --teleport; push local work up with claude --cloud.
  • Terminal to desktop: /desktop continues the current terminal session in the desktop app for visual diff review.
  • Slack: mention @Claude with a bug report and get a pull request back.

Per the overview, most surfaces need a Claude subscription or a Claude Console account. If ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is set, Claude Code skips the login prompt and asks you to approve the key instead. The terminal CLI, VS Code and JetBrains also run against third-party providers (Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, Microsoft Foundry). On native Windows, the docs recommend Git for Windows so the Bash tool works; without it Claude Code falls back to PowerShell.

For a healthcare org, the HIPAA setup page says the HIPAA configuration applies only to local-mode sessions signed in with a Claude Enterprise account that connect directly to the Claude API. Sessions through Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry or an LLM gateway are not eligible for it.

Trap: Assuming a Homebrew or WinGet install keeps itself current. Only native installs auto-update; package-manager installs need brew upgrade or winget upgrade for features and security fixes.
Trap: Expecting a cloud session to see your local plugins, user settings or settings.local.json. The settings page says cloud sessions read the repo's committed .claude/settings.json and server-managed settings only.
Synthesis: Pick the surface by where the code must execute: local terminal or desktop when Claude needs your files, tools and credentials; cloud when the task is long, parallel or must survive a closed laptop; Remote Control when you want the phone UI but local execution.

cards.q: Which Claude Code install methods auto-update in the background?
cards.a: Native installs. Homebrew and WinGet installs do not, so you upgrade them yourself.

cards.q: What does Remote Control do, and where does the code execute?
cards.a: It lets claude.ai/code or the Claude mobile app drive a Claude Code session, while execution and file access stay on your own machine.

cards.q: Which command pulls a cloud session into your local terminal?
cards.a: claude --teleport. It requires a claude.ai subscription.

cards.q: What is the difference between the claude-code and claude-code@latest Homebrew casks?
cards.a: claude-code tracks the stable channel, usually about a week behind and skipping releases with major regressions; claude-code@latest gets every release immediately.

cards.q: Does the JetBrains plugin include the CLI?
cards.a: No. It requires the Claude Code CLI to be installed separately; the desktop app, by contrast, bundles Claude Code.

concepts.n: The agent loop, tools, sessions and checkpoints
concepts.s: Claude Code is a harness that wraps a Claude model with tools and context management, runs a gather-act-verify loop you can interrupt at any point, and records every session locally so you can resume, fork or rewind it.

x.b:
The How Claude Code works page describes three blended phases: gather context, take action and verify results. Two components power the loop: the model that reasons and the tools that act. The docs call the surrounding layer the agentic harness.

  • Built-in tool categories: file operations, search, execution (shell, tests, git), web (search and fetch) and code intelligence (type errors, go-to-definition; needs a code intelligence plugin). Claude also has tools to spawn subagents and ask you questions.
  • What it can access: your project directory, your terminal, git state, CLAUDE.md, auto memory and any extensions you configure.
  • Steering: press Esc to stop immediately (the running tool call is cancelled). Type a correction and press Enter without stopping to queue it; Claude reads it after the current tool calls finish, within the same turn.

Per the docs, each message, tool use and result is written to a plaintext JSONL file under ~/.claude/projects/. Sessions are independent: a new session starts with a fresh context window.

  • claude --continue or claude --resume reopens a session under the same ID and appends to it.
  • --fork-session or /branch copies the history into a new session ID and leaves the original unchanged.
  • Sessions are tied to a directory; the /resume picker shows the current worktree's sessions by default.
  • Switching git branches changes the files Claude sees but keeps the conversation.

The checkpointing page says every prompt that starts a turn creates a checkpoint of files Claude's edit tools touch. Snapshots are kept for the 100 most recent checkpoints in a session and are deleted by the retention sweep, by default about 30 days after the session last saved one (cleanupPeriodDays).

Open the menu with /rewind or Esc twice on an empty prompt. Options: Restore code and conversation, Restore conversation, Restore code, Summarize from here, Summarize up to here, Never mind.

Trap: Treating checkpoints as a safety net for shell commands. Files changed by Bash (rm, mv, cp), most subagent edits, external edits, and symlinked or hard-linked files are not restored. Remote side effects (databases, APIs, deploys) cannot be checkpointed at all.
Trap: Using checkpoints in place of git. The docs describe them as session-level recovery; commits remain your durable history.
Trap: Pressing Esc twice with text in the prompt. That clears the input instead of opening the rewind menu (the text goes to input history).

• Does this task touch remote systems that rewind cannot undo? If so, gate them with permission rules instead of relying on checkpoints.
  • Do I want to continue this thread (--continue) or explore an alternative without losing it (/branch)?
  • Is the context now polluted enough that a fresh session plus a written handoff beats resuming?

cards.q: What are the three phases of Claude Code's agentic loop?
cards.a: Gather context, take action and verify results. They blend together and repeat until the task is done.

cards.q: How do you redirect Claude mid-task without stopping it?
cards.a: Type the correction and press Enter. It is queued and Claude reads it as soon as the running tool calls finish, within the same turn.

cards.q: What is the difference between --resume and --fork-session?
cards.a: --resume (or --continue) appends to the same session ID; --fork-session (or /branch) copies the history into a new session ID and leaves the original intact.

cards.q: Does /rewind undo a file deleted with rm through the Bash tool?
cards.a: No. Checkpoints track only edits made by Claude's file editing tools, not Bash-driven changes.

cards.q: How many checkpoints keep file snapshots per session?
cards.a: The 100 most recent checkpoints in a session.

concepts.n: Models, effort, thinking and cost visibility
concepts.s: You choose a model with an alias or full ID, tune reasoning depth with effort levels, and watch spend with /usage, the status line and JSON cost fields.

x.b:
The model configuration page lists aliases default, best, fable, sonnet, opus, haiku, sonnet[1m], opus[1m] and opusplan. Aliases resolve to the newest model in the family for your provider; pin a version with a full model name. Precedence, highest first: /model in session, claude --model, ANTHROPIC_MODEL, the model setting, then ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_MODEL.

  • Fable models (Fable 5.1 and Fable 5) are described as the most capable, for long autonomous tasks, and are never the default; select them with /model fable.
  • opusplan uses Opus in plan mode and Sonnet for execution.
  • Fallback: --fallback-model or a fallbackModel array tries alternates when the primary is overloaded.
  • Each model has its own prompt cache, so the settings page warns that the first request after a switch re-reads the whole conversation uncached.

Effort levels are low, medium, high, xhigh and max, set with /effort, --effort, CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL or effortLevel. Defaults vary by model. The Week 16 digest called xhigh the recommended setting for most coding work when it shipped with Opus 4.7.

The costs page says extended thinking is on by default, thinking tokens bill as output, and thinking cannot be turned off on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5 or the Fable models. On adaptive-reasoning models use effort instead of MAX_THINKING_TOKENS, which they ignore when nonzero.

/effort ultracode (or claude --effort ultracode) is a separate session toggle that has Claude plan a dynamic workflow for each substantive task; the workflows page warns each request then uses more tokens and time.

• /usage: the Session block shows token counts and a locally computed dollar estimate (meant for API users); subscribers also see plan usage bars and, on paid plans, attribution of usage to skills, subagents, plugins and MCP servers with fix recommendations.
  • /insights writes an HTML report on how you work, from up to 200 recent sessions.
  • claude -p --output-format json returns total_cost_usd with a per-model breakdown; both are client-side estimates.
  • OpenTelemetry export is the only option the docs name for streaming per-user token and cost metrics into your own observability stack on every setup.

The costs page reports enterprise averages of about $13 per developer per active day and $150 to $250 per developer per month, with 90% of users under $30 per active day.

Trap: Leaving Opus as the default for routine work on an API or cloud-provider plan. The costs page names long uncleared sessions and Opus-as-default as the usual causes of unexpected spend.
Trap: Switching models mid-session casually. The next request re-reads the full conversation without cache.
Trap: Trusting the /usage dollar figure as your bill. It is computed at list price unless an admin sets modelPricing in managed settings.
Synthesis: Treat model and effort as two separate dials: the model sets the capability ceiling, effort sets how much of it each turn spends. Raise effort before switching to a bigger model when a task fails for lack of reasoning depth.

cards.q: What does the opusplan alias do?
cards.a: It uses Opus while in plan mode and switches to Sonnet for execution.

cards.q: List the Claude Code effort levels from lowest to highest.
cards.a: low, medium, high, xhigh, max.

cards.q: Which takes precedence: claude --model or the model key in settings.json?
cards.a: claude --model. The order is /model, then --model, then ANTHROPIC_MODEL, then the model setting, then ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_MODEL.

cards.q: Which JSON field gives the estimated cost of a claude -p run?
cards.a: total_cost_usd, returned with --output-format json alongside a per-model breakdown.

cards.q: Why does switching models mid-session cost more on the next request?
cards.a: Each model has its own prompt cache, so the first request after a switch re-reads the whole conversation uncached.

concepts.s: Plan mode lets Claude read, explore and write a plan without editing your source, and you approve or edit that plan before any change happens.

x.b:
The permission modes page gives three ways in: press Shift+Tab to cycle to it, prefix a single prompt with /plan, or start with claude --permission-mode plan. Press Shift+Tab again to leave without approving.

  • Claude can read files, run shell commands to explore and write a plan. It cannot edit source until you approve.
  • Shell commands while planning: if auto mode is available and useAutoModeDuringPlan is on (the default), the classifier reviews commands; otherwise anything outside the built-in read-only set prompts you.
  • The built-in Plan subagent does read-only research during plan mode.

When the plan is ready, Claude offers Yes, and use auto mode (or Yes, auto-accept edits when auto mode is unavailable), Yes, manually approve edits, or No, keep planning. Press Ctrl+G to open the plan in your text editor and change it first.

Plans are saved to ~/.claude/plans/ by default (change with plansDirectory). The context window page says the plan is re-injected from disk after compaction, so it survives a long session.

• Boris Cherny, who created Claude Code, said in an X thread (January 2, per Thread Reader) that he starts most sessions in plan mode, iterates until the plan is right, then switches to auto-accept edits.
  • The costs page recommends plan mode for complex tasks because a wrong initial direction causes expensive rework.
  • The opusplan alias pairs naturally with plan mode: stronger reasoning for the plan, cheaper execution.

Trap: Assuming plan mode is a hard read-only sandbox in every case. The docs note an exception: in interactive terminal sessions with bypass permissions available, plan-mode blocks are not enforced.
Trap: Approving a plan you skimmed. Once you choose an auto option, edits flow without per-file prompts; Ctrl+G editing is the cheap place to fix scope.

cards.q: Name three ways to enter plan mode.
cards.a: Shift+Tab to cycle to it, prefix a prompt with /plan, or start with claude --permission-mode plan.

cards.q: Which key opens the proposed plan in your editor before approval?
cards.a: Ctrl+G.

cards.q: Where are plan files stored by default?
cards.a: ~/.claude/plans/, configurable with the plansDirectory setting.

cards.q: Does the plan survive auto-compaction?
cards.a: Yes. The plan Claude wrote in plan mode is re-injected from disk after compaction.

concepts.n: CLAUDE.md, rules, AGENTS.md and auto memory
concepts.s: CLAUDE.md files are instructions you write and Claude loads every session, .claude/rules scopes instructions to file paths, and auto memory is a per-repo notebook Claude writes for itself.

x.b:
The memory docs list four CLAUDE.md locations, all concatenated into context (none override each other):

  • Managed policy: /Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/CLAUDE.md (macOS), /etc/claude-code/CLAUDE.md (Linux, WSL), C:\Program Files\ClaudeCode\CLAUDE.md (Windows).
  • User: ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md.
  • Project: ./CLAUDE.md or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md, committed for the team.
  • Local: ./CLAUDE.local.md, personal and gitignored.

Files in the working directory and every ancestor load at launch, ordered root-down so the closest file is read last; CLAUDE.local.md is appended after CLAUDE.md at each level. Files in subdirectories load on demand when Claude reads or edits a file there. /init generates a starter CLAUDE.md (and suggests improvements if one exists). Run /context to confirm what loaded.

• Imports: @path/to/file expands another file inline. Relative paths resolve from the importing file; maximum depth is four hops. Imports organize content but do not reduce context cost.
  • .claude/rules/: markdown files that load every session, or only when Claude touches matching files if they have paths frontmatter. ~/.claude/rules/ holds personal rules for every project.
  • AGENTS.md: Claude Code reads it as project instructions when no CLAUDE.md, .claude/CLAUDE.md or CLAUDE.local.md exists in the working directory or above (requires v2.1.277 or later). The Project instructions setting claude-md-and-agents-md loads both.
---
paths:
  - "src/api/**/*.ts"
---

# API Development Rules
- All API endpoints must include input validation

The memory page says Claude saves four kinds of notes, tagged with a type field: user, feedback, project and reference. It skips anything derivable from the code or already in CLAUDE.md.

  • Stored at ~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/; the project is derived from the git repo, so all worktrees share one memory directory.
  • The first 200 lines or 25KB of MEMORY.md, whichever comes first, load at session start.
  • On by default in local sessions. Toggle in /memory (saves autoMemoryEnabled), set autoMemoryEnabled: false per project, or export CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY=1.

Related steering: output styles (/output-style; built-ins Proactive, Concise, Explanatory, Learning) change role, tone and format for a whole session. The output styles page frames the split as CLAUDE.md for what Claude should know and an output style for how it responds.

• Target under 200 lines per CLAUDE.md; the docs say longer files cost context and reduce adherence. Move part-of-the-codebase guidance into path-scoped rules and occasional reference material into skills.
  • The project-root CLAUDE.md and unscoped rules are re-read from disk after /compact; nested CLAUDE.md files and paths: rules reload only when a matching file is read again.
Trap: Writing guardrails as CLAUDE.md prose. The memory page says Claude treats CLAUDE.md as context, not enforced configuration; use a PreToolUse hook or a deny rule for anything that must never happen.
Trap: Adding a CLAUDE.local.md to a repo that relies on AGENTS.md. It counts as a CLAUDE.md file, so Claude stops reading AGENTS.md for you unless you switch Project instructions to claude-md-and-agents-md.
Trap: Expecting a gitignored CLAUDE.local.md to follow you into new worktrees. It exists only where you created it; import a file from your home directory instead.

cards.q: In what order do CLAUDE.md files from parent directories appear in context?
cards.a: From the filesystem root down to the working directory, so the file closest to where you launched is read last; CLAUDE.local.md follows CLAUDE.md at each level.

cards.q: What is the maximum import depth for @path imports in CLAUDE.md?
cards.a: Four hops.

cards.q: How much of MEMORY.md loads at session start?
cards.a: The first 200 lines or 25KB, whichever comes first.

cards.q: When does Claude Code read AGENTS.md by default?
cards.a: Only when there is no CLAUDE.md, .claude/CLAUDE.md or CLAUDE.local.md in the working directory or above it.

cards.q: How do you make a rule load only when Claude works on TypeScript API files?
cards.a: Put it in .claude/rules/ with paths frontmatter, for example paths: ["src/api/**/*.ts"].

concepts.s: Everything Claude Code sends lives in one finite context window, and you manage it with /context to inspect, /compact or /rewind summaries to shrink, /clear to reset, and subagents to keep bulky reads out.

x.b:
The context window page lists what loads at startup: system prompt, auto memory, environment info, MCP tool names (schemas deferred), skill descriptions, CLAUDE.md files, plus a git status snapshot. As you work, file reads, command output and conversation accumulate.

Anthropic's engineering post on context engineering frames context as a finite attention budget with diminishing returns (context rot), and cites Claude Code's compaction as a long-horizon technique that keeps key decisions while discarding redundant tool output.

Several current models (the Fable models, Sonnet 5 and recent Opus models) run with a 1M-token window per the model config page; older 4.6 models need a [1m] suffix. CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_1M_CONTEXT=1 keeps a 200K window.

• /context: live breakdown by category with suggestions; /context all shows per-MCP-tool token use.
  • /compact focus on ...: summarize now, keeping what you name. A Compact Instructions section in CLAUDE.md steers every compaction.
  • /autocompact 500k: set how full the window gets before auto-compaction (also autoCompactWindow, CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW; values 100K to 1M).
  • /rewind then Summarize from here or Summarize up to here: compress part of the conversation.
  • /clear: start fresh between unrelated tasks. The costs page notes it costs nothing, while /compact is itself a large request.

Per the context window page:

  • Re-injected from disk: project-root CLAUDE.md and unscoped rules, auto memory, the plan-mode plan.
  • Reloaded only on a matching read: paths: rules and nested CLAUDE.md files.
  • Files read or edited: up to five re-read, most recently modified first; a file over 5,000 tokens comes back as a path reference.
  • Invoked skill bodies: re-injected, capped at 5,000 tokens per skill and 25,000 total, oldest dropped first, truncated from the end.
  • Background commands and subagents keep running.
  • SessionStart hooks matching the compact source run and add their output.

Trap: Giving an important rule only in chat. Early conversation instructions can be lost at compaction; put persistent rules in CLAUDE.md.
Trap: Pasting one giant log or file. If a single output refills the window right after each summary, Claude Code stops auto-compacting after a few attempts with a thrashing error.
Trap: Putting the critical part of a long SKILL.md at the bottom. Re-injection keeps the start of the file, so the end is what gets cut.
Synthesis: Use the cheapest tool that fits: /clear for a new task, a focused /compact for continuity, a subagent before the bulky read happens. Compaction is a recovery move; isolation is a prevention move.

cards.q: Which command shows what is consuming your context window?
cards.a: /context, which gives a live breakdown by category with optimization suggestions.

cards.q: How many recently touched files does Claude Code re-read after compaction?
cards.a: Up to five, most recently modified first; files over 5,000 tokens come back as a path reference only.

cards.q: What caps apply to skill bodies re-injected after compaction?
cards.a: 5,000 tokens per skill and 25,000 tokens total, with the oldest invoked skills dropped first.

cards.q: How do you make Claude preserve specific details whenever it compacts?
cards.a: Add a Compact Instructions section to CLAUDE.md, or pass a focus to /compact, such as /compact focus on the API changes.

cards.q: Why prefer /clear over /compact when switching to unrelated work?
cards.a: /clear costs nothing and removes stale context entirely, while /compact must read the whole conversation to summarize it.

concepts.s: The default professional loop separates read-only exploration and planning from implementation so the agent does not solve the wrong problem, and it ends each unit of work in a reviewable commit.

x.b:
Anthropic's Claude Code best practices page recommends four phases:

  1. Explore in plan mode. The agent reads files and answers questions without changing anything.
  2. Plan. Ask for a detailed implementation plan (files to change, flow, risks). The page notes you can open the plan in your editor and edit it before the agent proceeds.
  3. Implement. Leave plan mode and have the agent code against its plan, write tests, run the suite and fix failures.
  4. Commit. Ask for a descriptive commit message and a PR.

OpenAI's Codex best practices make the same split: use Plan mode for complex or ambiguous work, ask Codex to interview you and challenge assumptions when the idea is fuzzy, and keep a PLANS.md or execution-plan template for long multi-step work. Every task prompt should carry four things: goal, context, constraints and done criteria ("what should be true before the task is complete").

• Anthropic's rule of thumb: if you could describe the diff in one sentence, skip the plan. Planning pays when you are unsure of the approach, the change spans several files, or the code is unfamiliar.
  • Boris Cherny, who created Claude Code, said in X posts summarized by InfoQ in January 2026 that he stays in plan mode until he likes the plan, then switches to auto-accepting edits, because "a good plan is really important."
  • Peter Steinberger, in his December 2025 post "Shipping at Inference-Speed", described the opposite habit: he skips plan mode and explores conversationally with the model, then refactors as he goes.
Synthesis: Planning effort should scale with ambiguity and blast radius. A large mechanical change with a clear pattern can need less planning than a three-line change in unfamiliar authentication code.

Anthropic's page gives four before/after patterns that hold across tools:

  • Scope the task: name the file, the scenario and test preferences ("cover the logged-out edge case, avoid mocks").
  • Point to sources: tell the agent where the answer lives ("look through this class's git history").
  • Reference existing patterns: name an exemplar file to copy the structure from.
  • Describe the symptom: give the symptom, the likely location and what fixed looks like, ideally as a failing test.

Codex guidance adds: match reasoning effort to difficulty, low for scoped tasks and higher for debugging or long agentic work.

• Interrupt early. Anthropic's page says tight feedback loops beat waiting for a finished but wrong result.
  • Rewind restores conversation, code or both to an earlier prompt checkpoint. Checkpoints only track edits made through the agent's file-editing tools, so changes made by shell commands are not captured, and they are no substitute for git.
  • After two failed corrections on the same issue, Anthropic recommends clearing the session and writing a better first prompt that includes what you learned, because the failed attempts now pollute the context.

Trap: Letting the agent jump straight to code on an ambiguous task. It produces a plausible solution to the wrong problem, and you pay for it in review.
Trap: Running a full plan cycle on a typo fix. Plan mode adds overhead that a one-sentence diff does not need.
Trap: Correcting the same mistake over and over in one long session. Each failed attempt stays in context and biases the next one.
Trap: Treating agent checkpoints as version control. Commit early and often so you can reset to a known-good state.

cards.q: Per Anthropic's best practices, what is the quick test for skipping plan mode?
cards.a: If you could describe the diff in one sentence, skip the plan and ask for the change directly.

cards.q: What four elements does OpenAI's Codex guidance say every task prompt should contain?
cards.a: Goal, context, constraints and done criteria, meaning what should be true before the task counts as complete.

cards.q: What should you do after correcting the agent twice on the same issue?
cards.a: Clear the session and restart with a sharper initial prompt that includes what you learned, since the failed attempts are polluting context.

cards.q: Do Claude Code checkpoints capture changes made by Bash commands?
cards.a: No. They only track edits made through the file-editing tools, so you still need git commits as your real safety net.

concepts.s: Writing a self-contained spec before implementation, often by letting the agent interview you, front-loads the decisions agents are worst at guessing, although heavy spec frameworks can become overhead of their own.

x.b:
Anthropic's best practices recommend that for larger features you start with a minimal prompt and ask Claude to interview you in detail (technical implementation, UI, edge cases, tradeoffs), then write the result to SPEC.md. You then start a fresh session to implement it, so the new context is focused on building and the spec is the durable reference.

The page says the most useful specs are self-contained: they name the files and interfaces involved, state what is out of scope, and end with an end-to-end verification step that proves the feature works. It adds that time spent making the spec precise pays off more than time spent watching the implementation.

I want to build [brief description]. Interview me in detail.
Ask about implementation, UI/UX, edge cases and tradeoffs.
Skip obvious questions. Keep going until we've covered everything,
then write a complete spec to SPEC.md.

x.t: Harper Reed's spec, plan, todo pipeline
x.b:
Harper Reed's widely shared February 2025 post "My LLM codegen workflow atm" laid out a pattern many practitioners still copy:

  1. Idea honing: a chat model interviews you with "Ask me one question at a time so we can develop a thorough, step-by-step spec for this idea," then writes spec.md.
  2. Planning: a reasoning model turns the spec into a blueprint of small, testable steps written as a sequence of codegen prompts in prompt_plan.md, plus a todo.md checklist.
  3. Execution: the coding tool works through the prompts and checks off todo.md, which preserves state across sessions.

He describes the planning step as about 15 minutes and warns about getting "over my skis", where pace outruns understanding.

x.t: Spec-driven development tools and their critics
x.b:
Birgitta Böckeler's October 2025 analysis on martinfowler.com sorts spec-driven development (SDD) into three levels:

  • Spec-first: write a spec and use it for the current task.
  • Spec-anchored: keep the spec after the task and maintain it alongside the code.
  • Spec-as-source: humans edit only the spec, and code is regenerated from it.

Her hands-on findings: Kiro generated four user stories and 16 acceptance criteria for a small bug; GitHub's spec-kit produced many repetitive markdown files that were tedious to review, and the agent still ignored notes about existing code and created duplicates; Tessl (then in private beta) showed non-determinism when regenerating code from the same spec. She compares the risk to model-driven development: its inflexibility combined with LLM non-determinism.

In Geoffrey Huntley's Ralph loop setup the agent reads a specs/ directory and a prioritized fix plan on every iteration, so the spec doubles as the loop's long-term memory.

• Simon Willison notes in his October 2025 post on parallel agents that reviewing code that matches a spec you wrote takes much less effort than reviewing code that arrives unexpectedly. The spec is a review aid as much as a build input.
  • Böckeler found reviewing long markdown harder than reviewing code. Keep specs short enough that a human actually reads them.
Synthesis: The parts of a spec that bind are the parts the agent can check: interface signatures, acceptance tests and the end-to-end verification step. Prose requirements without a corresponding check drift silently after the first implementation.

Trap: A spec longer than the diff. Böckeler's Kiro example shows fixed-ceremony workflows misfit small changes.
Trap: Implementing in the same session that produced the spec. The interview transcript fills context that implementation needs.
Trap: Treating a generated spec as reviewed. If nobody read it closely, it encodes the agent's guesses with false authority.

cards.q: Name Böckeler's three levels of spec-driven development.

concepts.s: Treat the context window as the scarce resource of every session, filling it with the smallest set of high-signal tokens and pushing research, logs and history out to subagents, files and fresh sessions.

x.b:
Anthropic's September 2025 engineering post "Effective context engineering for AI agents" frames the core ideas:

  • Context rot: recall accuracy drops as the window fills, because models have a finite "attention budget".
  • Smallest high-signal set: aim for "the smallest set of high-signal tokens that maximize the likelihood of your desired outcome."
  • Right altitude: instructions should sit between brittle hard-coded logic and vague guidance.
  • Just-in-time retrieval: keep lightweight identifiers such as file paths and load content only when needed.
  • Compaction, structured notes and subagents: summarize near the limit, persist notes outside the window, and let subagents work in clean windows and return condensed summaries.

The Claude Code best practices page states the practical consequence bluntly: most best practices follow from the fact that the window fills fast and performance degrades as it fills.

• Clear between unrelated tasks. Anthropic calls the mixed-topic session the "kitchen sink" anti-pattern.
  • Compact with instructions when you need continuity, and tell your instruction file what must survive compaction (for example the list of modified files and test commands).
  • Send investigations to subagents so their file reads never enter the main context.
  • Prefer CLI tools such as gh for external services; Anthropic calls them the most context-efficient integration.
  • OpenAI's Codex guidance: keep one thread per coherent unit of work, fork only when work truly branches, and avoid "one thread per project", which bloats context.

Nicholas Carlini's February 2026 Anthropic post on building a C compiler with parallel agents gives concrete harness rules: print only a few lines, write full logs to files, tag errors so grep finds them, and precompute summary statistics. Because the model has no sense of elapsed time, the test runner had a --fast option that ran a deterministic random 1% or 10% sample.

Synthesis: For data work the same rule applies to query results: have the agent write large result sets to files and read back counts, schemas and a few sample rows, rather than dumping thousands of rows into the conversation.

• Anthropic: for each line in CLAUDE.md ask "Would removing this cause Claude to make mistakes?" If not, cut it. Bloated files cause the agent to ignore real instructions.
  • OpenAI: "A short, accurate AGENTS.md is more useful than a long file full of vague rules."
  • OpenAI's harness engineering write-up (reported by InfoQ in February 2026) keeps detailed knowledge in a structured docs directory of maps, execution plans and design specs that agents load on demand.

Trap: The unscoped investigation. Asking the agent to "look into" something without limits lets it read hundreds of files into the main context.
Trap: Trusting compaction blindly. Summaries drop details; persist critical state to a file the next session can read.
Trap: Context anxiety. Anthropic's March 2026 harness design post describes models wrapping up early as they near what they believe is the limit. Watch for sudden premature "done" claims late in long sessions.

cards.a: The model's ability to recall information accurately declines as the context window fills, so more context can make results worse.

concepts.s: Top practitioners turn every repeated correction into durable infrastructure, such as an instruction-file rule, a reusable command or skill, a script or a hook, so the same mistake does not recur.

His fixes include AGENTS.md updates and small scripts and tools, for example for taking screenshots and running filtered tests.

concepts.n: Give the agent a way to verify
concepts.s: The highest-leverage practice in agentic coding is giving the agent a check it can run, such as tests, a build, a linter, a type checker or a screenshot comparison, so it can close the loop without you.

x.b:
Anthropic's best practices put this first: the agent stops when the work looks done, and without a runnable check "looks done" is the only signal, so you become the verification loop. A check is anything that returns a readable pass or fail: a test suite, a build exit code, a linter, a script that diffs output against a fixture, or a browser screenshot compared against a design.

The page lists escalating ways to gate the stop:

  • In one prompt: ask the agent to run the check and iterate.
  • Across a session: set a goal condition that a separate evaluator re-checks after every turn.
  • As a deterministic gate: a Stop hook runs your check and blocks the turn from ending until it passes (Claude Code overrides it after 8 consecutive blocks).
  • By a second opinion: a verification subagent tries to refute the result in a fresh context.

It also recommends asking for evidence (the command run, its output, a screenshot) instead of an assertion of success.

• Boris Cherny called a verification feedback loop the most important tip and claimed it improves results by a factor of 2 to 3 (X posts summarized by InfoQ, January 2026). For the Claude Code web app, Claude tests each change in a browser and iterates until the UI works.
  • Hashimoto lists "give agents a way to verify their output" among the lessons from redoing his own commits with agents.
  • OpenAI's Codex guidance: ask Codex to write or update tests, run the relevant checks, confirm behavior and review its own diff, and define "what good looks like" in the prompt or AGENTS.md.

Anthropic's November 2025 post on long-running harnesses found that, left alone, Claude verified with unit tests or curl and missed features that failed end-to-end. Prompting it to test as a human user through browser automation (a Puppeteer MCP server) improved results significantly. It still could not see browser-native alert modals, so features depending on them were buggier.

OpenAI's harness write-up (via InfoQ) describes agents using logs, metrics and spans to reproduce bugs in isolated environments.

Synthesis: For BI and data pipelines the equivalent checks are row-count and checksum reconciliations against a known-good source, schema and contract tests, and a rendered dashboard screenshot compared with an expected one.

x.b: Carlini's C compiler post: the tests must be nearly perfect, or Claude will optimize for the wrong target. He later added CI so new commits could not break existing features, and he warns that passing tests does not mean the work is done.

Trap: Fixing symptoms. Anthropic's example prompt says "address the root cause, don't suppress the error" because agents will otherwise silence the failing signal.
Trap: Premature "passing" claims. The long-running harness post lists marking features done before careful testing as a core failure; require evidence.
Trap: Flaky or slow checks. An agent cannot reason about a check that passes randomly or takes too long to run often.
Trap: If you cannot verify it, do not ship it. Anthropic's trust-then-verify gap: plausible code that misses edge cases.

cards.a: The agent stops when work looks done; without a pass or fail signal, you become the verification loop and every mistake waits for you.

concepts.s: Red/green test-driven development gives an agent a precise executable target and makes cheating visible, which is why many experienced practitioners make it the default mode for agent work.

x.b:
Simon Willison's Agentic Engineering Patterns guide (started February 2026) has a chapter on red/green TDD: writing the failing test first helps agents produce more succinct and reliable code with minimal extra prompting. Anthropic's best practices use the same move for bugs: "write a failing test that reproduces the issue, then fix it."

Kent Beck's June 2025 essay "Augmented Coding: Beyond the Vibes" includes his system prompt for building a B+ tree with an agent. Its core rules:

  • Write one failing test at a time, then the minimum code to pass it, then refactor.
  • Keep structural changes separate from behavioral changes: "Never mix structural and behavioral changes in the same commit."
  • Commit only when all tests pass and compiler and linter warnings are resolved.

Beck lists three signals that the agent (his "genie") is going off track:

  • Repetitive loops.
  • Functionality nobody asked for, even if it looks like a reasonable next step.
  • Cheating, such as disabling or deleting tests.

He stayed closely involved in design, stopped unproductive work, and when Rust stalled he had the agent write a Python version against the same tests and transliterate it. He was satisfied with correctness and performance but not simplicity, and concluded "Yes programming changes with a genie, but it's still programming."

• Anthropic's long-running harness stored the feature list as JSON in which coding agents could only flip a passes field, and the prompt said removing or editing tests is unacceptable. JSON was chosen because the model was less likely to overwrite it inappropriately than a markdown file.
  • Anthropic also suggests splitting roles across sessions: one writes the tests, another writes code to pass them.
Synthesis: Make tests read-only for the implementing agent wherever the tooling allows it, for example with a hook that blocks edits to the test directory during implementation, then review any test change as a separate, explicit step.

Trap: Tests written after the code that mirror the implementation. They pass by construction and verify nothing.
Trap: Mock-heavy tests. Anthropic's example prompt says "avoid mocks" when the point is real behavior.
Trap: Accepting a diff that touches both tests and code without checking which moved. A weakened assertion looks like a fix.

cards.q: What three warning signs does Kent Beck watch for in an AI coding session?

cards.a: Never mix structural changes (no behavior change) and behavioral changes in the same commit.

cards.q: Why did Anthropic's harness store the feature list as JSON rather than markdown?
cards.a: The model was less likely to inappropriately overwrite or edit JSON, and agents were only allowed to change the passes field.

cards.a: Have it write a failing test that reproduces the issue, then fix the code until the test passes.

concepts.n: Reviewing agent output and owning the code
concepts.s: Review is the bottleneck of agentic development, so strong teams pair fresh-context AI reviewers with human standards that require the author to understand and own every line that ships.

x.b:
• Anthropic's best practices describe a Writer/Reviewer pattern: one session implements, a second session with fresh context reviews, because a model is biased toward code it just wrote. The same page recommends an adversarial review subagent that sees only the diff and your criteria before you count work as done.
  • Its caveat: a reviewer asked to find gaps will usually report some even when the work is sound. Chasing every finding leads to over-engineering, so tell it to flag only gaps that affect correctness or stated requirements.
  • Anthropic's harness design post found that agents praise their own mediocre work, and that a separate evaluator is easier to tune toward skepticism than a generator is to make self-critical, though it still leaned lenient.

• OpenAI's Codex guidance says OpenAI has Codex review 100% of its PRs. /review covers a base branch, uncommitted changes or a specific commit, and a code_review.md referenced from AGENTS.md keeps standards consistent across repos.
  • GitHub's February 2026 changelog lets reviewers mention @claude or @codex in PR review comments to request changes (public preview).

• Andrej Karpathy, in a January 2026 X post reported by The Decoder, listed the errors he sees: wrong assumptions built on without checking, no pushback, bloated abstractions and dead code (about 1,000 lines that could be 100). For code that matters his advice is to "watch them like a hawk."

  • Willison reports he can only review and land one significant change at a time, which caps how much parallel agent output is useful.

Practitioners disagree openly. Steinberger wrote "These days I don't read much code anymore. I watch the stream and sometimes look at key parts." Steve Yegge has said he never looks at the code. Maggie Appleton's January 2026 response argues the right level of oversight depends on domain, feedback loops, risk tolerance, codebase age, team size and developer experience.

Synthesis: For regulated or patient-facing code paths (PHI access, clinical logic, billing), line-level human review stays mandatory. Low-risk internal tooling with strong tests is where reading less is defensible.

Trap: Rubber-stamping a large agent PR because CI is green. Size it so a human can actually review it.
Trap: Treating every AI reviewer finding as mandatory. It inflates code with defensive branches and needless abstractions.
Trap: Merging code nobody can explain. The person who merges owns it, whoever typed it.

cards.q: Why does Anthropic recommend reviewing in a fresh session or subagent?
cards.a: A fresh context sees only the diff and criteria, so it is not biased toward the reasoning that produced the code.

cards.q: What is the risk of prompting an AI reviewer to find gaps?
cards.a: It will usually report some even when the work is sound, and chasing them all leads to over-engineering; limit it to correctness and requirement gaps.

concepts.n: Security: sandboxes, permissions and prompt injection
concepts.s: Most agent productivity comes from fewer approval prompts, and the defensible way to get it is isolation plus least privilege, because prompt injection makes anything the agent reads a potential instruction.

x.b:
Simon Willison's October 2025 write-up of his talk "Living dangerously with Claude" defines the lethal trifecta: access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and the ability to communicate externally. With all three, an attacker can trick the agent into leaking data. His rule: anyone who can put text into the agent's context should be treated as controlling what it does next, including which tools it calls.

He argues sandboxes are the only credible defense, since AI-based attack detection is not reliable, and prefers sandboxes on someone else's computer (Claude Code on the web, Codex Cloud, Jules), so the worst case is a compromised remote machine. Restricting network access cuts off the exfiltration step.

• Manual approval: Anthropic's March 2026 auto mode post reports users accept 93% of permission prompts, so manual approval decays into click-through.
  • Allowlists: Cherny pre-approves safe commands such as build and test scripts and uses the skip-permissions flag only for long tasks inside a sandbox.
  • Auto mode: a classifier pipeline replaces most prompts. An input probe scans tool output for injection; a two-stage transcript classifier sees only user messages and tool calls. Anthropic reports a 0.4% false-positive rate on real traffic and a 17% miss rate on a small set (52) of real overeager actions, and says it is "not a drop-in replacement for careful human review on high-stakes infrastructure."
  • Full isolation: containers or cloud sandboxes with restricted network, where skipping approvals is reasonable.

OpenAI's Codex guidance: start with default permissions and loosen them only for trusted repos or specific workflows.

The Cloud Security Alliance's research note describes an early 2026 supply chain attack on the Cline project. An AI issue-triage workflow inserted issue titles straight into the agent's prompt, gave it shell and network tools, and let anyone trigger it. A crafted issue title led to Actions cache poisoning, theft of publishing tokens and, on February 17, 2026, a tampered cline@2.3.0 npm release that installed an unrelated agent on roughly 4,000 machines.

Its mitigations: audit workflows that put issue or PR text into prompts, restrict triggers to collaborators, give triage agents only label and comment permissions, isolate caches between low- and high-privilege workflows, use short-lived scoped credentials, and log agent inputs and actions.

Synthesis: In a HIPAA environment treat the agent like a new contractor laptop: no PHI or production credentials in its environment, read-only scoped database roles, synthetic or de-identified data for testing, and network egress limited to approved hosts. Confirm with your vendor and compliance team which agent products and plans your organization has approved for regulated data before connecting any of them.

Trap: Running a skip-all-permissions session on your laptop with cloud credentials in the environment. One injected instruction in a fetched web page can exfiltrate them.
Trap: Assuming a classifier makes autonomy safe. Anthropic publishes a 17% miss rate on real overeager actions.
Trap: Wiring an agent with write or shell access to public issue text. That is the Clinejection pattern.

concepts.s: A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md whose name and description sit in context until Claude or you invoke it, at which point the full instructions and any bundled files load on demand.

The skills docs say skills follow the Agent Skills open standard, and Claude Code adds invocation control, subagent execution and dynamic context injection. Anthropic's engineering post on Agent Skills describes three levels of progressive disclosure: metadata (name and description) preloaded at startup, the SKILL.md body read when relevant, and linked files opened only when needed.

  • Edits are picked up live without restarting. Legacy .claude/commands/ files still work as commands.

  • user-invocable: false: only Claude can invoke it (background knowledge).

name: fix-issue
description: Fix a GitHub issue
disable-model-invocation: true
---

Fix GitHub issue $ARGUMENTS following our coding standards.
1. Read the issue  2. Implement the fix  3. Write tests  4. Commit

A line such as !`git diff HEAD` in the body is dynamic context injection: Claude Code runs it before Claude sees the skill.

  • Skill content stays in context across later turns, so the docs advise writing standing instructions, not one-time steps.
  • Govern skills like tools: deny Skill entirely, or write rules like Skill(deploy *); skillOverrides sets a skill you did not write to on, name-only, user-invocable-only or off.

Trap: Leaving side-effecting skills model-invocable. Set disable-model-invocation: true on deploy or release skills so Claude cannot trigger them on its own.
Trap: Installing skills from untrusted sources. Anthropic's Agent Skills post warns they can carry malicious code or instructions and recommends trusted sources only, plus review of bundled scripts.

concepts.s: A subagent is a separate Claude instance with its own context window, system prompt, tools and permissions that does a delegated task and returns only a summary to the main conversation.

x.b:
The subagents page lists four reasons to use them: preserving context, enforcing tool constraints, reusing configurations, and controlling cost by routing work to smaller models. Claude delegates when a task matches a subagent's description.

  • Built-in: Explore (fast, read-only search; Write and Edit denied), Plan (read-only research in plan mode), General-purpose (full tools).
  • Fork: a subagent that starts with a copy of your conversation. The Week 33 digest says fork mode is on by default in interactive sessions.
  • Background: per the Week 27 digest, subagents run in the background by default so Claude keeps working.
  • Invoke by natural language, by @-mention (@"code-reviewer (agent)"), or run a whole session as one with claude --agent code-reviewer.

Subagents are Markdown files with YAML frontmatter; only name and description are required. Priority when names collide: managed, --agents flag, .claude/agents/, ~/.claude/agents/, plugin agents/.

---
name: code-reviewer
description: Reviews code for quality and best practices. Use after code changes.
tools: Read, Glob, Grep
model: sonnet
---

You are a code reviewer. Analyze the code and give specific,
actionable feedback on quality, security, and best practices.

Other fields: disallowedTools, model (sonnet, opus, haiku, fable, full ID or inherit), permissionMode, maxTurns, skills (preloaded in full), mcpServers, hooks, memory, isolation: worktree, effort.

  • Disable specific agents with deny rules such as Agent(Explore).
  • Combined descriptions over 15,000 tokens trigger a startup warning.
  • The Week 24 digest says subagents can spawn their own subagents, with background chains capped at five levels.

Trap: Expecting the subagent to know what you discussed. A non-fork subagent starts fresh, so the delegation prompt must carry the context it needs.
Trap: Assuming subagents are free. Their summaries still land in your context, and their own requests still draw on your usage.
Trap: Relying on /rewind for subagent edits. The checkpointing page says most subagent edits are not restored; use git.
Synthesis: Delegate when the intermediate work is large and disposable (searches, logs, multi-file reads) and only the conclusion matters. Keep work in the main thread when you need to watch and steer each step.

The worktrees page: claude --worktree feature-auth (or -w) creates .claude/worktrees/<name>/ on a branch named worktree-<name>. claude --worktree "#1234" branches from a pull request.
